title: Formed to bear it
hookLine: whatever happens, you're either made to bear it or not; if not, it will end (Meditations 10.3)

lines: A LONG NIGHT IN A WAITING ROOM.
cards: A long night in a hospital waiting room. A hard season at work. A grief that isn't going anywhere fast.
Someone tells you, you're stronger than you think. Sometimes that helps. Sometimes it feels like being handed a heavier box.
Marcus has his own version of that sentence in book ten of the Meditations, but his is stranger, and in an odd way more honest, because it has two halves.

teach.h: EITHER YOU CAN BEAR IT, OR NOT.
teach.b: Everything that happens, Marcus writes, happens either in a way you're formed by nature to bear, or in a way you're not.
If it's the kind you're formed to bear, don't complain. Bear it, as you were made to.
If it's the kind you're not formed to bear, don't complain either, because it will come to an end, once it has used you up. That's blunt, and it's meant to be honest.
For Marcus, nothing truly unbearable goes on forever; it has an end built into it.
Then he adds a further sentence: remember that you're formed to bear everything that your own judgment can make bearable, by thinking of it as in your interest, or as your duty.
In other words, a great deal of what feels impossible is made heavier by the story we tell about it. Change the story, and the weight can change. That isn't a promise for every pain.
Some pain is in the body, some is grief, and no story removes it. Nothing in this passage says you have to carry anything alone, either; asking for help is also a way of bearing.
But Marcus's question is worth keeping: which part of this weight is the thing itself, and which part is what I've told myself about it?

how: Stoic readers often separate a hardship into the event itself and the judgments added to it, and work on the judgments, while still seeking practical and medical help where it's needed.

o: a hard choice between right and wrong
a two-way split for meeting what happens
a sign your path has gone the wrong way

games.q: formed to bear it — tap the pairs.
p: it will come to an end
can make much of it bearable

s: Marcus promises that every pain can be thought away
he says judgment can make much bearable, not everything; and what can't be borne, he says, ends.
the entry has two halves: bear it, or know it will end
either way, he tells himself, don't complain.

games.q: something hard has happened. you're Marcus. what does book ten tell you to ask first?
o: am I formed to bear this, and how much is my judgment adding?
how can I avoid feeling anything?
games.why: everything is either bearable by nature or not, he writes; and you're formed to bear whatever your judgment can make bearable.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you've been carrying, a moderate weight, not the heaviest, and look at it in two parts: the thing itself, and the story on top of it, it's not fair, it'll never change, I can't.
Breathe, and see whether one piece of the story could be set down. Then ask whether you can bear this today; if not, remember it won't last forever, and that you can ask for help.
If a weight ever feels like too much, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, or call local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Fork. Marcus's structure for everything that happens: either you're formed to bear it, so bear it, or you're not, and it will end. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: to bear, to carry, the verb used for carrying a load.

carryVoice: Your line: made to bear it. Asking for help is part of bearing, too. Go gently.
